subject: Harris's hawk
title: This Hawk Hunts in Packs, and They Stand on Each Other's Backs

scenes.text: Almost every hawk hunts alone. One species hunts like a wolf pack.
Harris's hawks of the American Southwest live in groups, most often five birds, and they hunt as a team.
Some flush a jackrabbit out of cover while others wait in ambush. If it bolts, they chase it in relays.
They have to. A jackrabbit weighs more than twice as much as a female hawk, and three times a male.
Then there's the part nobody can fully explain. They stand on each other's backs.
Stacks five hawks high have been reported. Scientists still don't know why.

description:
Almost every bird of prey hunts alone. Harris's hawks hunt in packs.
In the 1980s ecologist James Bednarz radio-tagged about 40 Harris's hawks in the New Mexico desert and found they lived in groups, most often of five, and hunted together (Science, 1988). He described three tactics: the surprise pounce, the flush-and-ambush, in which some birds drive prey out of cover towards the others, and the relay attack, a chase that can run for more than half a mile. Teamwork lets them take jackrabbits, which weigh more than twice as much as a female hawk and more than three times as much as a male. The hawks also perch on each other's backs, for a few seconds or up to about 20 minutes; a stack five birds high has been reported, and the reason is still unknown.
Why do you think they stack up? Comment below.
first_comment: One hawk can stand on another's back for up to 20 minutes, and nobody knows why. What's your theory?
